findings.title: CyberService is a God class: 613 LOC, 10 repositories, 8 unrelated entity domains in one service
findings.cvss: Maintainability risk: a single class owning frameworks, controls, sub-controls, assessments, vulnerabilities, exceptions, incidents, assets, evidence and action plans concentrates change risk and merge conflicts; no runtime exploit but high regression surface.
findings.description: CyberService is a single @Service spanning 613 lines that injects 10 repositories (frameworkRepo, assetRepo, controlRepo, subControlRepo, assessmentRepo, vulnerabilityRepo, exceptionRepo, incidentRepo, evidenceRepo, actionPlanRepo — lines 25-34) and provides full CRUD plus workflow methods for EIGHT distinct domain concepts (frameworks, controls, sub-controls, assessments, vulnerabilities, exceptions, incidents, assets, evidence, action plans). Each domain has its own get/getAll/save/update/delete/workflow methods. This violates the Single Responsibility Principle: there is no cohesive reason these aggregates share a class beyond living under the same module. Compare with the vuln_sla and asm sub-packages, which split each concern into its own dedicated service (AttackSurfaceAssetService, AttackSurfaceFindingService, ShadowItService).
findings.rootCause: Module was built as one flat service before sub-package extraction (asm/, vuln_sla/, threatintel/) became the pattern. The core cyber service was never decomposed to match.
findings.evidence: 10 @final repository fields (lines 25-34); 8 domain regions each delimited by a banner comment (// Frameworks, // Controls, // Sub-Controls, // Assessments, // Vulnerabilities, // Exceptions, // Incidents, // Assets, // Evidence, // Action Plans); total 613 LOC measured with wc -l.
findings.impact: Every cyber feature change touches one file; high merge-conflict probability across teams; harder to unit-test a single domain in isolation; the class is the largest in all 5 audited packages.
findings.reproduction: wc -l tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java -> 613. Count @final repository fields -> 10. Count region banners -> 8 domains.
findings.resolution: Split CyberService into per-aggregate services (CyberControlService, CyberVulnerabilityService, CyberIncidentService, CyberAssetService, CyberEvidenceService, CyberActionPlanService, CyberAssessmentService) mirroring the asm/ and vuln_sla/ sub-package convention. Keep a thin CyberDashboardService for the cross-cutting getDashboard aggregation. The controller can fan out to the new services without API changes.

findings.title: Repetitive update/save/delete CRUD scaffolding duplicated across 8 entities in CyberService
findings.cvss: Maintainability only: the same five-line 'copy id/orgId/externalId/createdAt, force isDeleted=false, save' block is repeated per entity; a bug fix in the merge logic must be applied 8 times.
findings.description: The updateX(id, req) methods for CyberControl, CyberSubControl, ControlAssessment, Vulnerability, VulnException, CyberIncident, CyberAsset and CyberActionPlan are byte-for-byte identical except for the entity type: load existing, copy req.setId/setOrganisationId/setExternalId/setCreatedAt from existing, setIsDeleted(false), save. Likewise the deleteX(id) methods (8 copies of load + setIsDeleted(true) + save) and the saveX(entity, orgId) methods. This is the same 'reattach detached entity' merge pattern repeated ~24 times.
findings.rootCause: No generic base service / mapper helper for the org-scoped soft-deletable CRUD pattern that every BaseEntity child shares.
findings.evidence: updateControl (199-207), updateSubControl (240-249), updateAssessment (282-290), updateVulnerability (354-362), updateException (411-420), updateIncident (455-463), updateAsset (508-517), updateActionPlan (586-594) all repeat: req.setId(existing.getId()); req.setOrganisationId(existing.getOrganisationId()); req.setExternalId(existing.getExternalId()); req.setCreatedAt(existing.getCreatedAt()); req.setIsDeleted(false); return repo.save(req);
findings.impact: Any change to the merge contract (e.g. also preserving a new audit column) must be hand-applied to 8 methods; easy to miss one and create an inconsistency or a mass-assignment hole.
findings.reproduction: Diff updateControl against updateAsset / updateIncident in CyberService.java — only the type name and repository differ.
findings.resolution: Introduce a small protected generic helper, e.g. protected <T extends BaseEntity> T merge(T req, T existing, JpaRepository<T,Long> repo) that copies id/orgId/externalId/createdAt and forces isDeleted=false, or use a MapStruct mapper with @MappingTarget. Each updateX collapses to load + merge.

findings.title: PrivacyService swallows audit and event-bus exceptions with empty catch(Exception ignored) — no logging at all
findings.cvss: Operational visibility risk: a failing audit-log write or failing F8 event publish on the regulator-discharge path (SDAIA breach notification) is silently dropped with zero log output, so an audit-trail gap or broken automation goes completely undetected.
findings.description: recordSdaiaSubmission() wraps the F7 audit write and the F8 event publish in two try blocks each ending in `} catch (Exception ignored) { // ... }`. The catch bodies contain only a comment ('Audit failures must not block the regulator-discharge path.') and discard the exception entirely — no log.warn, no log.error, no stack trace, no cause. PrivacyService does not even declare a logger (no @Slf4j on the class). The intent (do not block the discharge path) is reasonable, but silently eating the exception means a persistent audit-sink outage or a serialization failure in the event payload is invisible in production logs. This is the textbook swallowed-exception anti-pattern on a compliance-critical PDPL Article 31 code path.
findings.rootCause: Best-effort side-effects (audit + event) were made non-fatal by catching broadly, but the author omitted any logging and the class lacks a logger.
findings.impact: A broken audit trail or non-firing BREACH_REPORTED_TO_SDAIA automation cannot be diagnosed from logs; for a regulator-facing 72-hour notification flow this defeats forensic accountability.
findings.reproduction: Stop the audit-log datastore and call recordSdaiaSubmission(); the breach still saves and returns 200 with no log line indicating the audit write failed.
findings.resolution: Add @Slf4j to the class and log at WARN with the exception inside both catch blocks: `log.warn("SDAIA audit write failed for breach {} — continuing", id, ex);`. Catch a narrower type if feasible. Keep the non-fatal behaviour but make the failure observable.
references: CWE-390 Detection of Error Condition Without Action

findings.title: VulnerabilitySlaController does business logic, injects a repository, and reads the user id by reflection with a swallowed exception
findings.cvss: Maintainability + correctness risk: the controller bypasses the service layer to query the repository and dereferences the security principal reflectively, so an API/refactor mismatch fails silently (returns null user id) and the dashboard aggregation logic lives in the wrong layer.
findings.description: Three distinct layering smells in one controller: (1) it injects VulnerabilitySlaFindingRepository directly (line 52) and the dashboard() endpoint runs seven count queries plus list calls and assembles the DashboardSnapshot itself (lines 160-176) — data-access and aggregation that belong in a service. (2) currentUserId() (lines 180-193) resolves the authenticated user's id via reflection: principal.getClass().getMethod("getId").invoke(principal), to 'avoid an extra dependency from this leaf module to the security package'. (3) that reflective call is wrapped in `catch (Exception ignored) { return null; }`, so any rename of GrcUserDetails.getId(), or a different principal type, silently yields a null actor id with no log — the remediation audit row then records by=null.
findings.rootCause: The module avoided a compile-time dependency on the security package by reflecting on the principal, and skipped the service layer for the read-heavy dashboard endpoint.
findings.evidence: Line 52: `private final VulnerabilitySlaFindingRepository findingRepo;` in a @RestController. Lines 161-167: seven `findingRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatusAndIsDeletedFalse(...)` calls in the controller. Lines 186-192: `try { var m = principal.getClass().getMethod("getId"); ... } catch (Exception ignored) { return null; }`.
findings.impact: Renaming/refactoring the principal accessor breaks user attribution with no error; dashboard query logic cannot be unit-tested without the web layer; controller and service responsibilities are blurred.
findings.reproduction: grep for `findingRepo` in the controller (line 52, 161-167) and `getClass().getMethod("getId")` (line 187). Change GrcUserDetails.getId() to getUserId() and observe currentUserId() returns null silently.
findings.resolution: Move the dashboard aggregation into VulnerabilitySlaComputeService (or a dedicated VulnSlaDashboardService) and drop the repository from the controller. Replace the reflective principal access with a typed cast to the security module's user-details type (add the dependency — it is the platform's own security package, not an external one) or inject an existing helper; on failure log at WARN instead of silently returning null.
references: Layered architecture — controllers must not access repositories
CWE-390 Detection of Error Condition Without Action

findings.title: SocOpsScheduledSweep: 10 near-identical sweep methods and a broad catch that logs only getMessage(), losing the stack trace
findings.cvss: Maintainability + diagnosability risk: the per-org sweep failure path catches Exception and logs only ex.getMessage() (no stack trace/cause), and the 10 sweep methods repeat the same loop/dedup/publish/markFired skeleton, so a NPE inside a sweep is hard to localize.
findings.description: Two related issues. (1) ERROR HANDLING: tick() wraps each tenant's full sweep in `catch (Exception ex) { log.warn("[socops sweep] org={} scan failed: {}", orgId, ex.getMessage()); }` (lines 130-131). Logging only ex.getMessage() at WARN discards the stack trace and cause, so a NullPointerException (message=null) prints '... scan failed: null' with no class, line, or origin sweep. The sibling scheduler VulnerabilitySlaScheduler does this correctly — `log.error("...", ex)` (line 69). (2) DUPLICATION: the ten private sweepX methods (sweepSecurityEventSla, sweepRegulatorResponseDue, sweepCyberInsuranceRenewals, sweepIamPrivilegedReviewsDue, sweepCryptoCertExpiry, sweepPentestRetestDue, sweepSeasonalOverlayActivated, sweepForensicsHoldDisposalDue, sweepAppsecSlaBreached, sweepDlpCriticalUnreviewed) all repeat the identical body: fetch rows, loop, `if (alreadyFired(...)) continue;`, publishEvent(DomainEvent.of(...)), markFired(...), fired++. ~12 call sites of alreadyFired confirm the repeated skeleton.
findings.rootCause: Each trigger was added by copy-paste of the previous sweep; the common loop was never abstracted. The catch was written for brevity without considering loss of the stack trace.
findings.evidence: Line 131: `log.warn("[socops sweep] org={} scan failed: {}", orgId, ex.getMessage());` — message only. 12 `alreadyFired(...)` call sites (lines 164,183,203,213,232,252,262,284,307,330,353,377) each in an otherwise-identical for-loop body across the 10 sweep methods.
findings.impact: A bug in any single sweep surfaces only as 'scan failed: <message-or-null>' with no stack trace, forcing a code read to find which of 10 sweeps failed; adding/changing the dedup+publish contract requires editing 10 methods.
findings.reproduction: Inspect tick() lines 130-131 vs VulnerabilitySlaScheduler line 69; diff any two sweepX method bodies — only the repository call, entity type string, and payload map differ.
findings.resolution: (1) Change the catch to log.error with the exception object: `log.error("[socops sweep] org={} scan failed", orgId, ex);`. (2) Extract a generic helper, e.g. `<E> int sweep(String entityType, List<E> rows, Function<E,Long> idOf, Function<E,String> triggerOf, Function<E,Map<String,Object>> payloadOf)` that owns the loop/alreadyFired/publish/markFired, so each sweepX becomes one call.

findings.title: SocOpsScheduledSweep.alreadyFired runs an unbounded per-entity audit scan inside every sweep loop
findings.cvss: Performance risk that grows with audit-log size: dedup is implemented as a full fetch of an entity's audit rows followed by an in-memory linear scan, executed once per candidate row per sweep, per tenant, hourly.
findings.description: alreadyFired() calls auditRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(org, entityType, entityId) — fetching EVERY audit row ever written for that entity — and then linearly scans them in Java for a matching action_type marker. It is invoked for every candidate row in all 10 sweeps. As the audit ledger accumulates history for long-lived entities (a SecurityEvent or CyberInsurance policy may collect dozens of audit rows over time), this materializes and scans an ever-growing list to answer a boolean that the database could answer with a single exists query.
findings.rootCause: Reused a generic audit finder instead of adding a targeted existsBy...AndActionType repository method.
findings.evidence: Lines 393-398: `List<AuditLogEntry> rows = auditRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(org, entityType, entityId); for (AuditLogEntry row : rows) { if (marker.equals(row.getActionType())) return true; } return false;` — loads all rows, scans in memory.
findings.impact: Sweep cost scales with cumulative audit history rather than open-item count; on a large tenant the hourly sweep does N_candidates full-history fetches, increasing DB load and GC pressure over the system's lifetime.
findings.reproduction: Read alreadyFired (391-399); note it fetches the full ordered list then iterates, called from 12 sites inside per-row loops.
findings.resolution: Add a repository method `boolean existsByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityIdAndActionType(Long org, String type, Long id, String actionType)` and have alreadyFired delegate to it, pushing the predicate to SQL and avoiding the materialized scan.
findings.patchAfter:
return auditRepo.existsByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityIdAndActionType(
    org, entityType, entityId, AUDIT_PREFIX + trigger);

findings.title: ThreatIntelCorrelationService.correlate is a 115-line high-branching method with a copy-pasted hit-builder for IP and HOSTNAME
findings.cvss: Maintainability only: the IOC-matching method is long and branches through a 4-way switch; the ASSET CorrelationHit construction is duplicated between the IP and HOSTNAME cases, so a field change must be made twice.
findings.description: correlate() spans 115 lines (56-170) and does: empty-input guard, build CVE index, build IP index, then a per-IOC for-loop containing a 4-arm switch (CVE/IP/HOSTNAME/default), then sort + count. The IP arm (lines 112-127) and the HOSTNAME arm (lines 133-148) build a CorrelationHit for an asset with an identical 10-argument new CorrelationHit(...) call and the same CRITICAL/HIGH regulatorEscalation check — only the matching predicate differs (exact ipIndex lookup vs hostname substring). jscpd independently flags this self-duplication (113-128 <-> 134-149, 16 lines).
findings.rootCause: The HOSTNAME case was added by copying the IP case; the shared asset-hit construction was never extracted to a helper.
findings.evidence: jscpd-report.json: ThreatIntelCorrelationService.java:113-128 duplicates 134-149 (16 lines). Both arms call `hits.add(new CorrelationHit(ioc.type(), ioc.value(), ioc.severity(), "ASSET", a.getId(), a.getAssetName(), null, a.getCriticality(), blendedSeverity(ioc.severity(), a.getCriticality()), a.getAssetName(), ioc.sourceFeed() == null ? req.feedName() : ioc.sourceFeed()))` and the same escalation check.
findings.impact: Adding a field to the asset-match hit (or changing the escalation rule) requires editing two places; the long method is harder to read and to test arm-by-arm.
findings.reproduction: Compare lines 110-128 with 129-149 in ThreatIntelCorrelationService.java; the new CorrelationHit(...) and escalation block are identical.
findings.resolution: Extract a private helper addAssetHit(List<CorrelationHit> hits, IndicatorOfCompromise ioc, CyberAsset a, CorrelationRequest req) that performs the escalation check and the hit construction, and call it from both the IP and HOSTNAME arms. Consider extracting the index-building blocks into separate methods to shorten correlate().
findings.patchBefore:
case "IP" -> { for (CyberAsset a : matches) { if (CRITICAL||HIGH) escalate; hits.add(new CorrelationHit(...10 args...)); } }
case "HOSTNAME" -> { for (CyberAsset a : assetList) { ...same escalate; hits.add(new CorrelationHit(...same 10 args...)); } }

findings.title: PrivacyService uses inline fully-qualified class names instead of imports and mixes constructor + field injection
findings.cvss: Readability only: no runtime impact; fully-qualified names inline and inconsistent injection style reduce legibility and diverge from the rest of the codebase's import-and-@RequiredArgsConstructor convention.
findings.description: PrivacyService is annotated @RequiredArgsConstructor and injects five repositories via final fields, but then adds three @Autowired(required=false) field-injected dependencies (bcast, auditLog, eventPublisher — lines 34-43), mixing two injection styles in one class. Throughout recordSdaiaSubmission/getSdaiaStatus it spells out fully-qualified names inline rather than importing them: java.time.LocalDateTime (multiple), java.util.Set.of (line 109), java.util.Map / java.util.HashMap / java.util.LinkedHashMap (168, 194), and com.tss.grc.module.platform.automation.event.DomainEvent (line 175). The rest of the audited services (CoiService, ComplaintService, VulnerabilitySlaComputeService) use clean imports and a single injection style.
findings.rootCause: The SDAIA workflow (Open Issue #006) was bolted onto an existing service with quick inline FQNs and optional field injection rather than refactoring imports.
findings.evidence: Line 109: `private static final java.util.Set<String> SDAIA_STATES = java.util.Set.of(...)`. Line 175: `new com.tss.grc.module.platform.automation.event.DomainEvent(...)`. Lines 34-43: three @Autowired(required=false) fields alongside the @RequiredArgsConstructor final fields.
findings.impact: Lower readability and inconsistency with sibling services; mixed injection makes the true dependency set less obvious and complicates constructor-based testing.
findings.reproduction: grep `java\.util\.` / `java\.time\.` / `com\.tss\.grc\.module\.platform` inside method bodies of PrivacyService.java; grep `@Autowired` -> 3 hits in a @RequiredArgsConstructor class.
findings.resolution: Add proper import statements for LocalDateTime, Set, Map, HashMap, LinkedHashMap and DomainEvent and use the short names. Decide on one injection style — prefer constructor injection for the optional collaborators too (Spring injects null/Optional) or keep them as documented optional fields, but be consistent.

findings.title: ComplaintService.generateQuarterlyReport is an 80-line method computing eight aggregates inline
findings.cvss: Maintainability only: a single method computes received/resolved/escalated counts, average resolution, two SLA-breach percentages, top category, and total compensation, then upserts — many independent calculations in one transactional method.
findings.description: generateQuarterlyReport(String) spans 80 lines and performs eight distinct aggregate computations over the complaint list (totalReceived, totalResolved, totalEscalated, avgResolution, ackBreaches+ackBreachPct, resBreaches+resBreachPct, byCategory top, totalCompensation) plus the report upsert and audit, all inline. The two SLA-breach calculations (lines 370-387) each contain a non-trivial nested ternary over null acknowledgedOn/resolvedOn. This is the highest-branching method in the consumer package and is harder to unit-test than the rest of the well-factored ComplaintService.
findings.rootCause: The report aggregation was written as one procedural block rather than decomposed into per-metric helpers.
findings.evidence: Method body lines 350-430 (80 LOC); eight separate stream/loop aggregations; nested ternaries at lines 372-374 and 378-380 for the breach predicates.
findings.impact: Each metric cannot be tested in isolation; the breach-percentage logic (the part most likely to be wrong) is buried mid-method; future SAMA report fields lengthen the method further.
findings.reproduction: Read ComplaintService.java:350-430; count the distinct aggregate computations (8) before the upsert at line 403.
findings.resolution: Extract per-metric helpers, e.g. ackBreachCount(List<Complaint>), resolutionBreachCount(List<Complaint>), topCategory(List<Complaint>), and have generateQuarterlyReport orchestrate them. This shortens the method and makes the breach logic independently testable.

findings.title: CyberService.getDashboard is a 73-line method performing 6 full-table loads and many stream passes inline
findings.cvss: Maintainability + minor performance: a single dashboard method eagerly loads all controls, vulns, incidents, assets, action plans and evidence for the tenant and runs ~15 separate stream filter/count passes over them inline.
findings.description: getDashboard(Long) is 73 lines. It calls findAllByOrganisationId on six repositories (controls, vulns, incidents, assets, action plans, evidence — lines 57,66,74,80,85,92) to pull entire tenant tables into memory, then runs roughly fifteen separate .stream().filter(...).count() passes plus four per-framework score computations (each scoreForFramework itself streams the controls twice — lines 134-145) and three additional paged recent-N queries. The counting could largely be pushed to repository count queries; at minimum the method should be decomposed per dashboard section.
findings.rootCause: Dashboard was assembled by loading full lists and counting in Java for expedience, in one monolithic method.
findings.evidence: Six findAllByOrganisationId calls (lines 57,66,74,80,85,92); ~15 stream counts (lines 59-104); scoreForFramework streams controls twice per framework x4 frameworks (lines 134-145, called 109-112).
findings.impact: On large tenants the dashboard pulls every control/vuln/incident/asset/evidence/action-plan row into memory each call; method length makes the aggregation hard to follow and to test section-by-section.
findings.reproduction: Read getDashboard (53-126); count repository findAll* calls (6) and stream count() passes (~15). scoreForFramework (132-147) streams the same list twice.
findings.resolution: Extract per-section private methods (e.g. populateControlStats, populateVulnStats) and/or replace the in-memory counts with repository count-by-status queries (countByOrganisationIdAndImplementationStatus, etc.). Compute the four framework scores in a single pass over controls rather than two passes per framework.
